Potential Avenues for Redress for AI-related Harms under the GDPR: A Visual Explanation
June 26, 2026 
/ 
Laura Lazaro Cabrera , Magdalena Maier
While the protection of fundamental rights is one of EU AI Act’s stated goals, it only provides for a limited number of remedies against the harmful impact of AI systems or models. Instead, it largely relies on the existence of effective pathways to redress for AI-related harms in other areas of EU law. Against this background, CDT Europe’s report A Long Road Ahead — Effective Remedies for Artificial Intelligence Harms in the European Union considers the different avenues enabled by core areas of EU law that offer individual protections and directly or indirectly apply to AI – data protection, equality and non-discrimination, consumer protection, and product liability – that may allow individuals to exercise their right to an effective remedy in cases of harm induced by AI systems.
In this second instalment of the series , we look at the opportunities afforded by the General Data Protection Regulation in providing redress for AI-related harms.
Flowchart: I suspect my data was used by an algorithm and I’ve been seriously affected by the resulting decision. What are my options?
As a tech-agnostic law, the General Data Protection Regulation applies to all technologies processing personal data, irrespective of how they might be labelled or characterised in European law. While the AI Act was deliberately conceptualised to address harms stemming from AI, the contours of the definitions of an “AI system” or a “general-purpose AI model” are either open to interpretation or subject to changes . This creates a gating issue: many algorithm-based technologies may not obviously meet the definitions set out in the AI Act, casting into doubt the applicability of the AI Act to the specific use case, and consequently complicating and delaying enforcement. The GDPR can play a crucial role in these edge cases where personal data is processed: its rights-based framework can offer an alternative avenue to access redress.
Automated decision-making and the right to an explanation
The GDPR recognised early on the risks involved in automated decision-making, banning the use of personal data for decisions based solely on automated processing, when such a decision would cause legal effects or significantly affect a data subject. In other words, the default position under the GDPR is that consequential decisions may not be taken through a fully automated process, irrespective of whether the process is AI or a simpler algorithmic system. This ban – while partial – is broader in scope than the bans articulated in the AI Act, and overcomes the gating challenge of having to prove that a technology meets the AI system definition in order to engage the AI Act’s prohibitions.
The prohibition is however not absolute, and creates three targeted exceptions where there is explicit consent by the data subject, the processing is necessary for entering into or performing a contract between the data subject and the entity processing the data, or when the processing is authorised by national or EU law subject to adequate safeguards.
Even in cases where the consent or contractual exceptions are met, the ban on automated decision-making lays down key safeguards, such as the right to human intervention, the right to be heard, and the right to contest a decision. Recent case-law from the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) recognised a further right in these circumstances, colloquially known as the right to an explanation . According to the CJEU, this right would require disclosure of meaningful information about the logic involved in a solely automated decision, opening up a key avenue for access to information that may enable informed contestation of the decision.
Interaction between the right to an explanation in the GDPR and the right in the AI Act
The AI Act creates an explicit right to an explanation when an individual considers that they are adversely impacted by a decision based on the output of an AI system in a set of specific use cases, exhaustively listed in the Annex III of the Act. The AI Act’s version of a right to explanation complements the GDPR’s: it does not require for a decision to be solely automated (unlike the GDPR) and allows a looser relationship between the output of an AI system and the decision ultimately taken, thus overcoming the challenge of an ornamental “human in the loop” whose presence – irrespective of whether their intervention is meaningful or not – would likely remove the processing from the scope of the GDPR prohibition on automated decision-making. Conversely, the AI Act approach limits the applicability of the right to an explanation to a finite set of deployments of AI systems – classified as “high-risk” in the law – essentially subordinating the exercise of the right to a prior assessment of whether the AI system in question meets the high-risk criteria. One final point of note is that the AI Act’s right to an explanation applies to the extent that it is not otherwise provided for under EU law, leading scholars to point to a “hydraulic” relationship between the AI Act and other laws including the GDPR, where the stronger interpretation of pre-existing explanation rights results in a narrower interpretation of the AI Act’s. The interpretation of this particular aspect of the right to an explanation will require further discussion and analysis in order to ensure that existing mechanisms are mutually reinforcing instead of weakening.
